column1: Why does the dot product measure similarity?
column2: a·b = |a||b|cos θ - maximal when aligned, zero when orthogonal, negative when opposed; normalized it's cosine similarity.

column1: What happens if you stack linear layers with no nonlinearity?
column2: W2(W1x) = (W2W1)x - composition of linear maps is one linear map; depth adds no expressive power.

column1: Eigenvectors in one sentence, and one ML place they appear?
column2: Directions a matrix scales without rotating (Av = λv); top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix are the PCA axes.

column1: Eigendecomposition vs SVD?
column2: Eigen needs square (orthogonal eigenvectors only if symmetric); SVD exists for any rectangular matrix - rotate–stretch–rotate; truncated SVD = best low-rank approximation.

column1: Why does L1 give sparsity but L2 doesn't?
column2: L1 ball has corners on the axes, so optima land at exact zeros; L1's pull toward 0 is constant-magnitude while L2's fades ∝ w near 0.

column1: Backprop in two sentences?
column2: Forward computes and caches intermediates; backward walks the graph in reverse, multiplying upstream gradient by each local derivative, summing where paths merge. One backward sweep gets all parameter gradients for ~one forward pass's cost.

column1: What is a Jacobian and its role in backprop?
column2: The m×n matrix of partials ∂fi/∂xj - the local linear map; backprop propagates vector–Jacobian products without materializing it.

column1: Why do gradients vanish or explode in deep nets?
column2: Backward signal is a product of per-layer Jacobians; singular values consistently below/above 1 make it decay/grow exponentially with depth.

column1: Gradient of ||Xw − y||², and what does setting it to 0 give?
column2: 2Xᵀ(Xw − y); zero gives the normal equations XᵀXw = Xᵀy - closed-form least squares.

column1: Derive Bayes rule in one line.
column2: Joint factors both ways: P(A|B)P(B) = P(B|A)P(A); divide by P(B).

column1: Why is minimizing cross-entropy the same as maximum likelihood?
column2: NLL of a probabilistic classifier with one-hot labels is exactly the cross-entropy loss. (MSE = MLE under Gaussian noise; L1 under Laplace.)

column1: Test with 99% sensitivity, 95% specificity, 1% prevalence, you test positive - roughly P(sick)?
column2: ~17%, not 99%: per 100k people, 990 true positives vs 4,950 false positives from the healthy 99% (base-rate neglect). At 99%/99% it would still be only 50%.

column1: Why divide by n−1 in sample variance?
column2: Deviations are from the sample mean, which chases the data - /n underestimates σ² by (n−1)/n; Bessel's correction unbiases it.

column1: Why does averaging reduce noise, and at what rate?
column2: Var(mean) = σ²/n, so standard error shrinks as 1/√n - 4× the data for half the error; CLT makes the mean ~Gaussian.

column1: Accuracy 91.0% → 91.5% on 1,000 test examples. Real?
column2: No - SE ≈ √(p(1−p)/n) ≈ 1%, so 0.5% is within noise; need a bigger test set, paired test, or multiple seeds.

column1: Why does least squares correspond to Gaussian noise?
column2: NLL of y = wᵀx + ε, ε∼N(0,σ²) is const + Σ(y−wᵀx)²/2σ² - minimizing NLL is minimizing squared error.

column1: Normal equation vs gradient descent - when each?
column2: Normal equation: small/medium d (O(nd² + d³)), exact, no LR. GD/SGD: large n or d, streaming, or no closed form.

column1: Gradient of logistic loss?
column2: (p − y)x - the sigmoid's p(1−p) cancels against the loss's derivative; no vanishing gradient from the sigmoid.

column1: Bayesian interpretation of ridge and lasso?
column2: MAP with Gaussian prior (ridge) or Laplace prior (lasso); regularizer = −log p(w).

column1: What is C in an SVM?
column2: Penalty on margin violations - inverse regularization (λ ~ 1/C). Large C: narrow margin, overfit risk; small C: wide margin, more bias.

column1: What does the kernel trick buy you?
column2: The dual touches data only via inner products; K(x,z) = ⟨φ(x),φ(z)⟩ runs the linear algorithm in a huge feature space without computing φ. Price: O(n²) Gram matrix.

column1: Gini vs entropy - does it matter?
column2: Rarely - both concave impurity measures picking nearly identical splits; Gini skips the log, so it's the cheap default.

column1: Why do random forests subsample features on top of bagging?
column2: Var(mean) = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B - trees kill the second term but the correlation floor ρσ² remains; feature subsampling decorrelates trees, lowering ρ.

column1: Bagging vs boosting in one line each?
column2: Bagging: parallel deep trees averaged to cut variance; more trees never overfit. Boosting: sequential shallow trees fit to pseudo-residuals to cut bias; can overfit - early-stop.

column1: In what sense is gradient boosting "gradient descent"?
column2: Descent in function space: predictions are the parameters, pseudo-residuals are the negative gradient, each weak learner approximates that vector, F ← F + ηh is the step.

column1: Why does k-means always converge, and to what?
column2: Each phase exactly minimizes J over one block (assignments, then means), so J is non-increasing and bounded - finite convergence to a local optimum; hence k-means++/restarts.

column1: Why standardize for kNN/k-means/SVM/regularized models but not trees?
column2: Those depend on Euclidean distance or penalized weight magnitude - scale-sensitive; trees only threshold one feature at a time, invariant to monotone transforms.

column1: Curse of dimensionality with one number?
column2: Capturing 1% of uniform data in [0,1]¹⁰⁰ needs a cube of side 0.01^(1/100) ≈ 0.955 - "local" spans 95% of every axis; distances concentrate.

column1: PCA: variance maximization or reconstruction minimization?
column2: Both - provably identical: ||x − UUᵀx||² = ||x||² − ||Uᵀx||²; solution = top covariance eigenvectors; lost energy = discarded eigenvalues.

column1: Why does logistic regression fail on perfectly separable data?
column2: MLE doesn't exist - scaling w up forever keeps increasing likelihood, weights diverge; regularization or early stopping restores a finite solution.

column1: Hinge vs logistic loss?
column2: Both convex upper bounds on 0–1 loss. Hinge: exactly zero past margin 1, only support vectors matter, no probabilities. Logistic: smooth, never zero, calibrated probabilities.

column1: Where does the 37% out-of-bag figure come from?
column2: P(point missed by all n bootstrap draws) = (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368 - free held-out error estimate per tree.

column1: Why can't you run plain SVD on a ratings matrix?
column2: It's ~99% missing; SVD optimizes error over ALL entries, so zeros-as-missing fits "everyone dislikes everything". Sum error over observed entries only + regularization → SGD or ALS.

column1: Why do neural nets need nonlinear activations?
column2: Composition of linear maps is linear - without nonlinearities any depth collapses to one linear layer; can't represent XOR or curved boundaries.

column1: Why is backprop efficient vs per-parameter finite differences?
column2: Finite differences: one forward pass per parameter. Backprop: the loss is scalar, so one reverse sweep gets all gradients - dynamic programming over the graph, ~2–3 forward passes total.

column1: Derive the softmax + cross-entropy gradient.
column2: L = −z_t + log Σe^{z_j}, so ∂L/∂z_k = p_k − y_k. The softmax Jacobian's mess cancels against −1/p_t from the log.

column1: Why not MSE for classification?
column2: MSE keeps a σ′-type factor (p(1−p)) that → 0 when confidently wrong - tiny gradient exactly when you need the biggest correction; CE cancels it, giving p − y.

column1: Sigmoid's maximum derivative, and the consequence for depth?
column2: 0.25 (at s = ½) - d sigmoid layers scale gradients by ≤ 0.25^d: vanishing gradients; hence ReLU, good init, normalization, residuals.

column1: What is a dead ReLU and how do you prevent it?
column2: Pre-activation negative for every input → output 0, gradient 0, never recovers (usually a huge update knocked the bias negative). Prevent: sane init, moderate LR/warmup, LeakyReLU/GELU.

column1: Derive Xavier and Kaiming init.
column2: Var(z) = n_in σ_w² Var(x); keep the factor 1 per layer → σ_w² = 1/n_in (Xavier: 2/(n_in+n_out)); ReLU halves the second moment → He's σ_w² = 2/n_in.

column1: Why not initialize with zeros?
column2: Every neuron computes the same output and gets the same gradient - symmetry never breaks; the layer acts as one neuron. Random init breaks it; Xavier/Kaiming set its scale.

column1: Adam in one line, and why bias correction?
column2: EMA of gradients (m) and squared gradients (v), step η·m̂/(√v̂+ε). EMAs start at 0 so early estimates are low; dividing by 1−βᵗ unbiases - without it, step 1 is ~30× too large via v.

column1: Weight decay vs L2 - same thing?
column2: Under plain SGD yes; under Adam no - L2's λθ gets divided by √v̂, under-regularizing high-gradient params. AdamW decouples the decay; transformer default.

column1: What does BatchNorm do and why does it help?
column2: Standardize per feature with batch stats, then learned γ,β. Best-supported story: smooths the loss landscape → larger LRs, less init sensitivity; plus mild noise regularization.

column1: Why does BatchNorm differ train vs test?
column2: Inference can't depend on batch-mates (or batch size 1), so it uses running EMA stats - a fixed affine map. Forgetting `model.eval()` is the classic silent bug.

column1: Why LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm in transformers?
column2: LN normalizes across features within one example - no batch dependence: handles variable-length/padded sequences, tiny sharded batches, and batchless autoregressive decoding; identical train/test.

column1: How does dropout work, and why scale by 1/(1−p)?
column2: Zero each unit w.p. p in training, scale survivors by 1/(1−p) so the expected input is unchanged - inference becomes an exact no-op. Prevents co-adaptation; approximates a 2ⁿ subnetwork ensemble.

column1: Why do residual connections help deep training?
column2: Block Jacobian is I + ∂F/∂h - gradient reaches early layers with factor exactly 1 along the skip path; forward view: start at identity, learn small corrections.

column1: Training loss is NaN after a few hundred steps - first suspects?
column2: (1) LR too high; (2) unstable log(softmax) - use log-sum-exp; (3) exploding gradients - clip, check init; (4) bad data (NaN/inf); (5) missing ε in a division. Bisect by logging ‖g‖ per layer.

column1: Why minibatches rather than full-batch?
column2: Gradient SE shrinks 1/√B while cost grows ∝ B - past modest B, compute buys more steps, not better steps; batches saturate hardware; gradient noise escapes saddles and finds flatter minima.

column1: How do you verify a hand-written backward pass?
column2: Centered finite differences (h ≈ 1e−5, O(h²) error) vs analytic gradient, relative error ≲ 1e−6 in float64, on a tiny model/batch.

column1: Why do CNNs use so many fewer parameters than MLPs on images?
column2: Weight sharing + locality: conv params C_out(C_in k² + 1) - independent of image size; the architecture hard-codes translation equivariance the MLP would have to learn from data.

column1: Conv output size and parameter count?
column2: H_out = ⌊(H + 2p − k)/s⌋ + 1; params = C_out(C_in k² + 1).

column1: Why did ResNet skips enable 150+ layers?
column2: Plain deep nets underfit (optimization failure - stacked layers can't represent identity); y = x + F(x) makes identity the default and puts I in every Jacobian.

column1: Derive why RNN gradients vanish/explode.
column2: ∂h_t/∂h_{t−1} = diag(tanh′)W_hh; over n steps the norm behaves like (γσ_max(W))ⁿ - geometric decay below 1, growth above; nothing pins it at 1.

column1: How does the LSTM fix vanishing gradients?
column2: Additive cell state: c_t = f⊙c_{t−1} + i⊙c̃, so ∂c_t/∂c_{t−1} ≈ diag(f) - no repeated W, no squashing; forget gate ≈ 1 is a data-dependent gradient highway. Doesn't fix exploding (still clip).

column1: Write down attention and gloss each part.
column2: softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V - queries (what a token seeks) dot keys (what tokens advertise), scale, softmax to a distribution, convex combination of values. A soft differentiable dictionary lookup.

column1: Why divide by √d_k?
column2: qᵀk with unit-variance entries has variance d_k (std 8 at d_k=64) - softmax saturates one-hot, Jacobian → 0, gradients vanish at init; scaling restores unit variance.

column1: Why does attention need positional encodings?
column2: Pure content-based dot products are permutation equivariant - "dog bites man" ≡ "man bites dog"; RNNs get order from sequence, CNNs from kernel layout. Fix: absolute embeddings or RoPE/relative bias.

column1: What do multiple heads buy over one big head?
column2: h independent attention distributions per token, each in its own learned subspace (dims split, so same compute) - one head can track position while another tracks coreference.

column1: Explain the KV cache. Why doesn't it help training?
column2: Causality means past K/V never change - cache them; each new token computes only its own q,k,v: O(td) per layer instead of O(t²d). Training computes all positions in one parallel pass and weights change every step - nothing to reuse.

column1: Complexity of self-attention?
column2: O(T²d) compute, O(T²) attention-matrix memory per head (FlashAttention removes the memory, not the FLOPs); MLP adds O(Td²); quadratic dominates once T ≳ d.

column1: Pre-LN vs post-LN - why does it matter?
column2: Post-LN normalizes the residual path - no identity path survives depth, needs warmup, unstable. Pre-LN (x + f(LN(x))) keeps the stream addition-only, I in every Jacobian - stable at depth.

column1: What does perplexity 20 mean?
column2: PPL = e^(mean CE in nats): the model is as uncertain as a uniform choice among 20 tokens - effective branching factor. Only comparable under the same tokenizer.

column1: Temperature vs top-k vs top-p?
column2: Temperature rescales logits (reshapes the whole distribution); top-k keeps the k most likely (fixed nucleus); top-p keeps the smallest set with mass ≥ p (adaptive). Compose: temperature then top-p.

column1: What is BPE and why not characters or words?
column2: Iteratively merge the most frequent adjacent pair from bytes up to a vocab budget. Characters: long sequences (quadratic pain); words: huge vocab + OOV. BPE interpolates, byte fallback means nothing is OOV.

column1: Why has RoPE replaced learned absolute positions?
column2: Rotating q,k by position-proportional angles makes the score depend exactly on the gap n−m by rotation algebra - relative structure shared across positions, defined at any length, extrapolates better.

column1: Why grouped-query attention?
column2: KV-cache size scales with KV heads; sharing one K,V per group of query heads cuts cache h/g× (4× at 32 heads, g=8) while keeping all h query subspaces - faster bandwidth-bound decode, bigger batches.

column1: An "8×7B" MoE - what runs per token and why bother?
column2: Router picks top-2 of 8 expert MLPs: own ~47B params, spend ~13B of FLOPs. Loss scales with params, cost with FLOPs - conditional compute buys params without per-token compute. Costs: all params in memory, routing comms, load-balancing loss.

column1: Precision and recall - define, and one case where each is priority.
column2: Precision = TP/(TP+FP): of the flagged, how many real - spam filtering. Recall = TP/(TP+FN): of the real, how many flagged - cancer screening.

column1: Why is F1 the harmonic mean, not arithmetic?
column2: Harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller value - predict-all-positive at 1% prevalence gets P=.01, R=1: arithmetic says 0.505, harmonic says ≈0.02 (correctly terrible).

column1: What exactly does AUC = 0.9 mean?
column2: A random positive is scored above a random negative 90% of the time - a ranking statement, independent of threshold, prevalence, and calibration.

column1: Fraud at 1:1000, AUC 0.98 - done?
column2: No - ROC axes are prevalence-free. With TPR=.9, FPR=.01, π=.001, precision ≈ 8%: most alerts false. Report PR curve / precision at required recall.

column1: Can AUC be 1.0 with terrible calibration?
column2: Yes - 0.51 for every positive, 0.49 for every negative: perfect ranking, meaningless probabilities. AUC sees order; calibration is about values.

column1: Temperature scaling - why doesn't it change accuracy?
column2: Dividing logits by T > 0 is monotone - argmax and the whole ranking (hence AUC) unchanged; only probability values move.

column1: State the bias–variance decomposition.
column2: E[(y − f̂)²] = bias² + variance + σ² - systematic error of the family, fit's sensitivity to the sample, and irreducible label noise.

column1: Does more data reduce bias or variance? Regularization?
column2: More data: variance. Regularization: variance down, some bias added.

column1: Test MSE below σ² - what does it mean?
column2: A bug or leakage - σ² is irreducible label noise, present regardless of model.

column1: Three forms of data leakage?
column2: (1) Preprocessing fit on full data before splitting; (2) target leakage - feature caused by the label; (3) temporal leakage - random splits on time series. (Bonus: same user in train and test.)

column1: Why nested CV?
column2: Reporting the best hyperparameter's CV score selects the max of noisy estimates - winner's curse. Inner loop selects, outer loop scores on folds never used for selection.

column1: A: 84.7%, B: 84.2%, same test set - ship A?
column2: Not yet - use a paired test (McNemar / paired differences) to remove shared example-difficulty variance, and multiple seeds: seed variance alone often exceeds 0.5%.

column1: What does a class weight do to the gradient?
column2: ∂L/∂z = w_y(p̂ − y) - minority examples push w× harder (≈ oversampling in expectation); side effect: calibration destroyed, recalibrate or move the threshold instead.

column1: Threshold moving vs resampling - when each?
column2: If probabilities are fine and only the decision is miscosted: keep natural training, set t* = c_FP/(c_FP + c_FN). Resample only when the minority is too rare to learn at all - then recalibrate.

column1: Prove the constant minimizing MAE is the median.
column2: h′(c) = P(y<c) − P(y>c); zero where both are ½ - the median. (MSE's zero gradient gives the mean.)

column1: Offline AUC up 2%, A/B flat - name causes.
column2: Ranking gains on pairs users never see; training/serving skew; offline label ≠ online goal; feedback loops (logs collected under the old policy). Trust the experiment, audit the proxy.

column1: LLM-judge biases and mitigations?
column2: Position (judge both orders), verbosity (length-control), self-preference (other-family judge/panel); then validate the judge against a human-labeled sample before trusting deltas.

column1: Why do recommenders use two stages instead of one great model?
column2: Arithmetic: even 1µs/item over 10⁹ items is 10³ s/request. Cheap ANN retrieval cuts 10⁹ → 10³ in ~10ms; the expressive model runs only there.

column1: What structural constraint defines a two-tower model, and the trade?
column2: Score must be f(u)·g(i) - no interaction before the dot product. Buys precomputed item embeddings + ANN retrieval; costs cross features (ranking stage handles those).

column1: Data drift vs concept drift?
column2: Data drift: P(x) moves, P(y|x) fixed - retrain on recent data. Concept drift: P(y|x) moves (fraud tactics shift) - retraining helps only after new-concept labels arrive; need proxies + rules.

column1: Training/serving skew - most common cause?
column2: The feature implemented twice (batch pipeline vs serving service) and diverging. Fix: single feature definition materialized to both stores + log served features and diff.

column1: What is point-in-time correctness?
column2: Every training feature computed only from data timestamped before that example's prediction time - else label leaks in, offline inflates, online craters. Enforced by as-of joins.

column1: Why is accuracy wrong for fraud, and what's right?
column2: At 0.2% fraud, always-legit is 99.8% accurate. Use precision/recall at threshold, PR-AUC, money-weighted recall, calibration (the decision is an expected-value computation).

column1: How do you handle position bias in click labels?
column2: Clicks confound relevance with exposure. Position as a training feature frozen at serving; inverse-propensity weighting from randomization; or examination × relevance factorization.

column1: Shadow vs canary vs A/B - what does each uniquely tell you?
column2: Shadow: latency/feature-availability at real traffic, zero outcome signal. Canary (1–5%): guardrail harms with fast rollback. A/B: the only stage that measures improvement.

column1: Why does bigger batch call for bigger LR?
column2: k× batch cuts gradient variance k× and gives k× fewer updates - take proportionally larger steps (linear scaling), with warmup because the rule fails early and at extreme k.

column1: Batch vs online inference - when batch?
column2: When inputs are enumerable in advance and hours of staleness is fine: precompute nightly, serve from a KV store. Online is forced when the input exists only at request time.

column1: Why does RAG exist instead of fine-tuning or paste-everything?
column2: Fine-tuning: slow per update, unreliable for verbatim facts, can't cite. Paste-all: context limits, linear cost, attention degradation. Retrieval: knowledge updates = index updates, answers carry citations.

column1: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
column2: Decompose: retrieval recall@k against gold passages; generation faithfulness-to-context + correctness on a golden set + abstention on unanswerables; online deflection/feedback.

column1: What do you monitor when labels arrive 60 days late?
column2: Label-free layers: per-feature distributions (nulls, PSI, unseen categories) and prediction distributions, sliced by segment; fast proxy labels; true metrics by maturity cohort.

column1: Features stable but online performance decaying - what and why?
column2: Concept drift signature: P(x) stable, P(y|x) moving. Confirm via calibration decay on freshest labels; respond with faster labels, recent-window retrains, rules meanwhile.

column1: PM asks for "just one metric" - answer?
column2: One primary online metric + guardrails that must not regress + a counter-metric for the primary's known failure mode; a single unguarded metric gets Goodharted.

column1: 10²³ FLOPs - what model do you train?
column2: Chinchilla: C = 6ND, D ≈ 20N → C = 120N², N = √(C/120) ≈ 29B params, D ≈ 580B tokens. Caveat: heavy serving traffic → overtrain a smaller model instead.

column1: Derive C = 6ND.
column2: Forward: 2 FLOPs per param per token; backward: two matmuls per forward matmul → 4N; total 6N per token × D tokens.

column1: Training memory for 70B with Adam, mixed precision?
column2: 16 B/param (2 fp16 weights + 2 grads + 4 fp32 master + 4 m + 4 v) → 1.12 TB of state + activations; ≥14 H100s, only with ZeRO-3/FSDP.

column1: Why fp32 master weights?
column2: The update ηg (~1e−6) is below the fp16 ulp near weight magnitude - it rounds to zero; accumulate in fp32, round to fp16 for matmuls.

column1: ZeRO stages - what does each shard?
column2: 1: optimizer state (12B/param); 2: + gradients; 3: + weights (16Ψ/G - the only stage fitting 70B on 80 GB GPUs, at ~1.5× DP communication). FSDP ≈ ZeRO-3.

column1: Where do all-reduces land in tensor parallelism?
column2: Column-split first matmul (comm-free), row-split second → one all-reduce per MLP block and per attention block, forward and backward; frequent and unhideable → TP stays inside a node's NVLink.

column1: Pipeline bubble fraction?
column2: (p−1)/(m+p−1) for p stages, m microbatches - p=8, m=32 gives 18%; raise m to amortize; 1F1B caps live activations.

column1: How does gradient checkpointing get O(√L) memory?
column2: Store k checkpoints, recompute L/k-layer segments in backward: peak ∝ k + L/k, minimized at k=√L; cost ≈ +33% FLOPs (one extra forward of the 6N).

column1: Batch 256 → 2048 - what happens to LR?
column2: Linear scaling: 8× with warmup (fails early in training); watch the critical batch size; for Adam √8× is often better.

column1: Derive DPO from the RLHF objective.
column2: KL-regularized reward max has closed form π* ∝ π_ref e^{r/β}; invert for r, substitute into Bradley–Terry - Z cancels, leaving a supervised loss on preference pairs. RM + RL collapse into one loss.

column1: Why the KL term in PPO-RLHF? Why the clip?
column2: KL-to-reference: the RM is only valid near the SFT distribution - unpenalized optimization reward-hacks it. Clip: bounds each update from stale samples (trust-region-lite).

column1: GRPO vs PPO?
column2: GRPO deletes the value network: sample G completions per prompt, advantage = (reward − group mean)/std - fits sparse verifiable rewards, saves an LM-sized critic.

column1: LoRA - why so cheap, and inference cost after training?
column2: Freeze W, learn ΔW = (α/r)BA with r ≪ d: r(d+k) params instead of dk (~250× fewer at 4096/r=8); B=0 init starts at the pretrained model; merge W + BA → zero added latency.

column1: How would you detect benchmark contamination?
column2: 13-gram overlap with training corpus, canary strings, verbatim-completion probes, accuracy drop on fresh matched-difficulty items (strongest), paraphrase sensitivity.

column1: Why is single-stream decode memory-bound?
column2: Decode is GEMV: ~1 FLOP per byte of weights read vs ridge ~156 (A100) - every token streams all weights; batching/speculation raise intensity, quantization shrinks bytes.

column1: Tokens/sec ceiling for 7B fp16 on 2 TB/s?
column2: bandwidth / weight bytes = 2e12 / 14e9 ≈ 143 tok/s.

column1: KV-cache size formula?
column2: 2 (K and V) × n_layers × d_model × bytes/value × seq × batch. 7B, batch 32, 4k ctx, fp16: 512 KB/token → ~69 GB - 5× the weights.

column1: Three ways to shrink the KV cache?
column2: GQA (÷ group factor, e.g. 8), KV quantization to int8/fp8 (÷2), PagedAttention (reclaims 60–80% fragmentation waste).

column1: Why does speculative decoding not change the output distribution?
column2: Accept draft x∼q w.p. min(1, p/q), else resample from (p−q)⁺ normalized: P(x) = min(p,q) + max(0, p−q) = p(x) exactly. Acceptance = 1 − TV(p,q).

column1: Is FlashAttention approximate?
column2: No - exact. IO reorganization: tile K,V through SRAM with online softmax, never materializing the T×T matrix in HBM; attention is bandwidth-bound, so ~10× less HBM traffic gives 2–4× speed and O(s) memory.

column1: What breaks in naive int8 quantization of LLMs?
column2: Outlier activation channels 20–100× larger dominate the absmax scale, crushing everyone else's resolution; fix with per-channel/group scales, mixed decomposition (LLM.int8), or scale migration (AWQ).

column1: Why is generation slow when training is parallel?
column2: Training teacher-forces all T positions in one masked pass; generation is sequential (token t+1 needs sampled token t) - n dependent forward passes, each bandwidth-bound.

column1: Why doesn't the KV cache help training?
column2: Every K/V is used immediately and exactly once per step, and weights change every step - nothing valid to reuse.

column1: Judge win-rate up 10 points - what do you check?
column2: Position/verbosity/self-preference biases, human agreement on a sample, fresh prompts, per-category breakdown, length drift - +10 win-rate with +40% length is a length gain.

column1: Quantization error trick that makes 4-bit GPTQ ≈ fp16?
column2: Quantize weights one at a time and update the remaining weights to absorb each rounding error instead of letting errors accumulate.

column1: Why does batching fix decode's bandwidth problem?
column2: One weight-stream serves B tokens - arithmetic intensity scales with B, moving decode toward the compute-bound regime.

column1: Bytes per parameter: fp32 / fp16-bf16 / int8 / int4?
Training bytes per parameter, mixed-precision Adam?
column2: 16 (2+2+4+4+4); ~20 with fp32 gradient accumulation. Say "16–20 before activations."

column1: Inference bytes per parameter, fp16?
column2: 2 - a 7B is ~14 GB, a 70B ~140 GB.

column1: Training compute rule?
column2: C = 6ND FLOPs (2 forward + 4 backward per param per token).

column1: Chinchilla-optimal tokens for N params?
column2: D ≈ 20N - so C ≈ 120N².

column1: A100 ballparks: bf16 compute, HBM bandwidth, ridge point?
column2: ~312 TFLOP/s, ~2 TB/s, ridge ≈ 156 FLOPs/byte.

column2: ~+33% FLOPs (one extra forward of the 6N total) for O(√L) activation memory.

column2: ~1% of revenue/engagement (the classic Amazon/Google findings) - why the latency budget is designed before the model.

column2: 2·4096·16 per matrix × 2 matrices × 32 layers ≈ 8.4M ≈ 0.12% of 7B.

column2: √(p(1−p)/n) - ~1% at n=1000, p≈0.9: half-point gains on 1k examples are noise.

column1: Sliding window - the invariant and the precondition?
column2: Window [l, r] satisfies predicate P; P must be monotone under shrinking, so the smallest valid l never moves left - l only advances, O(n) amortized.

column1: When does sliding window break, and the fallback?
column2: Negatives with sum predicates - shrinking no longer monotone. Fall back to prefix sums + hashmap (or monotonic deque for shortest-subarray-≥k).

column1: Two pointers - what licenses skipping pairs?
column2: An elimination argument: moving l must provably kill every pair (l, x) - one comparison + monotonicity discards a whole row of the pair matrix.

column1: Prefix-sum identity, and the hashmap trick for "subarray sum = k"?
column2: sum(i..j) = pre[j+1] − pre[i]; count earlier prefixes equal to pre[j+1] − k, hashmap seeded {0:1} for subarrays starting at 0. Query before insert.

column1: Binary search boundary invariant?
column2: Everything < lo is F, everything ≥ hi is T; the first T lies in [lo, hi]; loop `lo < hi`, moves `hi = mid` / `lo = mid + 1`, answer is lo.

column1: The `lo = mid` infinite-loop rule?
column2: The pointer assigned bare `mid` must be unreachable by the rounding: round down when `hi = mid`, round up (`+1` inside) when `lo = mid`.

column1: Binary search on the answer - recognition cue and the script?
column2: Minimize the maximum / "smallest value such that ⟨checkable⟩". Name the bracket, prove monotonicity in one sentence, write the (usually greedy) checker, drop in the boundary template.

column1: Rotated sorted array - what survives rotation?
column2: Cut anywhere and at least one side is properly sorted - a sorted half answers "is target in you?" in O(1), so discard half each step. Find-min: compare a[mid] to a[hi].

column1: Why does LIFO fit matching/nesting problems?
column2: In well-nested input, the thing that must close next is the thing that opened most recently - LIFO order IS nesting order.

column1: Monotonic stack - invariant and the O(n) argument?
column2: Stack holds the unanswered, monotone by construction (next-greater ⇒ decreasing); each index pushes and pops at most once, so the nested while is O(n) total.

column1: Floyd cycle detection - why must fast and slow meet?
column2: Inside a cycle of length C the gap changes by exactly 1 per step (mod C) - a quantity decreasing by 1 in a finite cyclic group hits 0; they can't jump over each other.

column1: LRU cache - derive the data structure from O(1) requirements.
column2: O(1) get ⇒ hashmap; O(1) recency reorder + evict-oldest ⇒ doubly linked list with sentinels; map values are the DLL nodes. Each covers the other's blind spot.

column1: The BST invariant, exactly?
column2: For every node, ALL keys in the left subtree < node < ALL keys in the right subtree - whole subtrees, not just children; validate by carrying (lo, hi) bounds down.

column1: The one tree template?
column2: Recurse on both subtrees, combine at the root; design questions: base case, combine, and is the answer at the root or anywhere (→ nonlocal best, return the local quantity).

column1: Heap: the property, the array trick, and Python's quirks?
column2: Every node ≤ children (min at root, siblings unordered); complete tree in an array, parent (i−1)//2, children 2i+1/2i+2; heapq is min-only - negate for max, add a counter to tuples for unorderable items.

column1: Why does BFS with a queue find shortest paths?
column2: FIFO processes all distance-d nodes before any d+1 - the expanding-rings order is the proof, for unweighted graphs.

column1: Kahn's algorithm - and how does it detect cycles for free?
column2: Peel indegree-0 nodes; if fewer than n ever reach indegree 0, the leftovers all have a prerequisite among themselves - a cycle.

column1: Union-find - the two optimizations and the result?
column2: Union by rank (height ≤ log n: a rank-r tree has ≥ 2^r nodes) + path compression → near-constant amortized find/union for incremental connectivity.

column1: Dijkstra - why is greedy safe, and its precondition?
column2: Cut argument: any shorter path to the closest unsettled node would cross the settled boundary at a node with even smaller tentative distance - contradiction. Requires non-negative weights.

column1: The universal DP checklist?
column2: State in words (checkable by hand) → recurrence as a decision ("what was the last move?") → base cases → evaluation order → where the answer lives. Cost = #states × transition cost.

column1: The 1-D knapsack compression bug?
column2: Iterating capacity ascending reads dp entries already updated for THIS item - item taken twice (that's the unbounded variant); 0/1 needs descending capacity.

column1: When is greedy trustworthy?
column2: Only with an exchange argument: any optimal solution can be swapped, one step at a time, into the greedy one without getting worse (e.g. earliest-finish interval scheduling). Guilty until proven safe.

column1: Merging intervals - the invariant after sorting by start?
column2: Once sorted by start, a new interval can only overlap the CURRENT last merged interval (start ≥ every earlier start) - so one pass: extend the last if start ≤ its end, else append. O(n log n) for the sort.

column1: Meeting Rooms II - two equivalent views of "minimum rooms"?
column2: Min-heap of end times (pop if the earliest end ≤ next start, heap size peak = rooms) or sort all endpoints and sweep +1/−1 tracking max concurrency - both compute the peak overlap count.

column1: RandomizedSet - why hashmap alone fails, and the O(1)-delete trick?
column2: getRandom needs index access (hashmap can't), delete needs O(1) (array can't from the middle). Combo: array + value→index map; delete = swap target with the LAST element, pop, fix the moved element's index.

column1: Two's complement: why does -x = ~x + 1, and what does x & (x−1) do?
column2: x + ~x is all 1s = −1, so ~x + 1 = −x. x & (x−1) clears the lowest set bit (the −1 borrows through the trailing zeros) - Kernighan popcount loops once per set bit; x & −x isolates that bit.

column1: Why does XOR-fold find the single number?
column2: XOR is commutative/associative, a⊕a = 0, a⊕0 = a - fold the array and every pair annihilates, leaving the singleton. Same trick finds the missing number: XOR all values with all indices.

column1: Rotate a matrix 90° clockwise in place?
column2: The index map (i,j) → (j, n−1−i) factors into transpose then reverse each row - two clean in-place passes; never try to spiral-swap by hand under time pressure.
